messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: geometry? negative binomial model unstable
parts:
The negative binomial malloc/free error case is more puzzling.
We hadn't ever used the negative binomial before (at least not
in BUGS examples), so it hasn't been field tested.

The following model winds up with alpha, beta going to +infinity
then segfaulting on a bad free (the seg fault needs to be fixed
as well as the model's bad behavior).

data {
int<lower=1> N;
int<lower=0> y[N];
}
parameters {
real<lower=0.0> alpha;
real<lower=0.0> beta;
}
model {
for (i in 1:N)
y[i] ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta);
}

And here's the data:

y <- c(0, 1, 4, 0, 2, 2, 5, 0, 1)
N <- 9

The sample mean is 5/3.

This is similar to what I get from Stan if I
hard code the scale term alpha = 1 (that is, beta
around 3/5).

Even so, it's still unstable and has memory errors
with different seeds.

If I constrain alpha and beta to be above 0.1, it doesn't
crash, but adaptation takes forever and the values
of alpha and beta still tend to +infinity.

If I constrain alpha, beta to the interval (0.1,10),
everything runs fine and the estimates for alpha range
from around 1 to around 9.5 with betas around the
sample mean.

If I only constrain on (0,10), I get problems
with memory again (perhaps NaN issues on
some kind of underflow?)

Everything's also stable if I reparameterize to
probability of success and use a strong enough
location=0.5 beta prior.

Is this another geometry issue?

- Bob

gets really small (e-21) and beta gets really big (e+24).

I've narrowed it down to lgamma crashing for a var passed in with a
value of -1.0. This happens when neg_binomial() is called with n = 0,
alpha = e-21, beta = e+24. This calls binomial_coefficient_log() with
-1, 0.

I'll try to figure out what's causing the crash.

of R's dump format. I have some specific
comments below.

> Regarding stan dumps I've been using my own function to write the dumps that adds some functionality and resolves

You probably just want to use RStan, which won't
have most of these problems, as we read the data
directly from the R environment without dumping
it (through Rcpp).

I'm going to put many of the following on the
C++ to-do list, along with treating single values
as length-one arrays. I really would like this to
flexibly handle R output.

> * catches the following errors
> o variable does not have a valid Stan name

This will just involve periods, or is there more?

> o variable does not exist

That's on the R side.

> o variable includes NA or NaN

NA is R only, and we have no way of supporting it
in Stan. At least not without major work.

I see that R just writes the string "NaN" (without the
quotes). I should update the C++ to handle that.

> o variable is not numeric

Also on the R side.

> * add a precheck option like base::save

What does this mean?

> * Replace Inf and -Inf with largest and smallest floating point numbers.

R just writes "Inf" and "-Inf", so again I should
be able to handle those on the C++ side.

> * Ensure integers are not printed with scientific notation

I should also handle this on the C++ side.

> * Written as a S4 generic function to accept either a character vector of object names or a list of objects.

That's just on the R side.
> I attached the code below.

Thanks.

More on code contributions in a separate e-mail.

- Bob

Since this issue is brought up, I guess at least we should know that in R, objects (even an element of a vector) can have names.  So in the R dump file, there might be names, which I think we could neglect.  An example:

> a <- 1:5
> names(a) <- 1:5
> dump("a", file = 'a.rdump')
> cat(paste(readLines('a.rdump'), collapse = '\n'), '\n')
a <-
structure(1:5, .Names = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5"))

--
Jiqiang

You probably just want to use RStan, which won't
have most of these problems, as we read the data
directly from the R environment without dumping
it (through Rcpp).

I've been holding off on using rstan seriously until it stabilizes.  The lack of saving compiled objects had been a deal breaker. But now that that's implemented, I'll probably move away from the command line interface.

I'm going to put many of the following on the
C++ to-do list, along with treating single values
as length-one arrays.  I really would like this to
flexibly handle R output.

>   * catches the following errors
>       o variable does not have a valid Stan name

This will just involve periods, or is there more?
Periods, not ending in __, and not being a C++ / Stan reserved name.   There's also a function that works like make.names in R, but will make valid Stan names.

>       o variable does not exist

That's on the R side.

>       o variable includes NA or NaN

NA is R only, and we have no way of supporting it
in Stan.  At least not without major work.

I see that R just writes the string "NaN" (without the
quotes).  I should update the C++ to handle that.

>       o variable is not numeric

Also on the R side.

>   * add a precheck option like base::save

It just checks for the existence of the objects, that they are numeric, and that they have valid names, before writing to the file. I noticed that save() had that option and it seemed like a good idea.

What does this mean?

>   * Replace Inf and -Inf with largest and smallest floating point numbers.

R just writes "Inf" and "-Inf", so again I should
be able to handle those on the C++ side.

>   * Ensure integers are not printed with scientific notation

I should also handle this on the C++ side.

>   * Written as a S4 generic function to accept either a character vector of object names or a list of objects.

That's just on the R side.
